title: Concept Map
description: Mapping between jj concepts and their git counterparts. jj is built on top of git, but some concepts differ.
mapping.0.explanation: A change in jj is a logical unit of work identified by a change ID. The change ID remains stable even after amend or rebase. In git, the commit hash changes.
mapping.1.explanation: jj has 3 types of IDs: (1) Change ID: immutable ID attached to a change, doesn't change even when you edit files, used by humans for tracking. (2) Commit ID: same as git's commit hash, changes every time you save. (3) Operation ID: assigned per jj operation, used with jj op restore. Git only has commit hash, which changes on amend.
mapping.1.jjExample:
change: ozuwwwmu (immutable)
commit: acd93feb (changes on save)
op: 717391bc3cae (operation record)
mapping.1.gitExample:
commit hash: 3b81a57e (changes on amend)
no other IDs
mapping.2.explanation: In jj, the working copy itself is a commit. There is no staging area. Changes to files are automatically reflected in the commit. No git add needed.
mapping.2.gitExample: git status / git add / git commit
mapping.3.explanation: A jj bookmark is a named pointer equivalent to a git branch. However, in jj it doesn't move automatically when new commits are made. You need to explicitly set it.
mapping.3.gitExample: git branch main / git checkout -b main
mapping.4.explanation: jj records all operations on the repository. Any operation can be undone/restored. Git's reflog only records branch movements, but jj records all state changes.
mapping.5.explanation: Commits that cannot be modified. By default, only the root commit. trunk() and remote bookmarks also become immutable. Shown with ◆ mark in jj log.
mapping.6.explanation: A query language for selecting revisions. Far more expressive than git's revision syntax. Also supports set operations (union, intersection, difference).
mapping.7.explanation: Same name but different meaning. git commit creates a new snapshot and generates a new hash. jj commit closes the current change and moves to the next new change. In jj, the change ID already exists from jj new, so commit doesn't create a new ID. Essentially a shortcut for jj describe + jj new.
mapping.7.jjExample:
jj commit -m "done"
= jj describe -m "done" + jj new
→ Close existing change, move to new change
mapping.7.gitExample:
git add -A && git commit -m "done"
→ New commit hash is created
mapping.8.explanation: Finalizes current changes (as parent) and creates a new empty working copy. Similar to git commit, but in jj the WC is already a commit, so it's like moving on top of a new commit.
mapping.9.explanation: Absorbs working copy changes into the parent commit. Similar to git amend, but safer because the change ID doesn't change.
mapping.10.explanation: A state where the same change ID has diverged into multiple commits. Shown with ?? mark in jj log. Often occurs when jj describe and automatic snapshot happen simultaneously. Git doesn't have this concept since commit hashes are immutable. A problem arising from jj's unique "change ID is immutable" property.
mapping.10.jjExample:
sxvmlnny?? 46fe29bd (no desc)
sxvmlnny?? a55e5b1a feat: ...
→ Two commits with same change ID
mapping.10.gitExample:
(doesn't occur)
git's commit hash is always unique
mapping.11.explanation: A format where jj and git coexist in the same directory. Both .jj/ and .git/ exist. You can use both git and jj commands. jj uses this format by default.
mapping.12.explanation: In jj, you can commit even with conflicts. You can commit with conflicts and resolve them later. In git, you cannot commit until conflicts are resolved.
mapping.12.jjExample: jj new main && jj rebase -d feature (conflict OK)
